title: Tool‑Augmented Post‑Processing of Identical LLM Candidates for Intent‑Driven Network Configuration (shared_initial_candidate evaluation)
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) that isolates the effect of deterministic post‑processing (a topology‑aware verifier + lightweight simulator) on deterministic validator pass/fail outcomes when the exact same single LLM candidate is reused verbatim across both arms (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Planned: 300 paired tasks; completed: 598 episodes → 299 analyzable pairs. For those 299 pairs the archived contingency is n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0: both baseline and guarded pipelines accepted the identical candidates in every analyzable pair. Paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10k resamples, seed=1729). All raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, and full SHA‑256 manifests are archived (execution/*; see Disclosure). The result is narrowly scoped: under shared_initial_candidate semantics post‑processing did not change deterministic‑validator verdicts for identical candidates. We document execution accounting, the single missing pair (pair‑000269) as a recorded provider failure (artifact paths and SHA‑256 in the execution manifest), and discuss ceiling effects, threats to validity, and concrete follow‑up designs required to evaluate tool‑augmented generation rather than post‑processing alone.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to convert operator intent into low‑level network configuration. Real‑world deployments commonly layer deterministic validators and simulators beneath generative agents to catch misconfigurations and enforce workflow constraints. Prior studies frequently conflate improvements due to (A) better generation and (B) downstream validation/repair. Our study isolates (B) by fixing generation: each task produced one LLM candidate that was reused verbatim by both experimental arms. The preregistered primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) asks whether applying deterministic post‑processing to an identical candidate changes the deterministic‑validator pass/fail outcome. We executed a fully archived, preregistered pipeline (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1), recorded every provider call and validator trace, and analyzed according to a frozen analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1).
sections.related_work: Intent→configuration and LLM‑for‑NetOps work motivate the architecture and evaluative focus: intent translation and small‑model fine‑tuning for network config (Nguyen et al., 2024, doi:10.1002/nem.2313), pretrained configuration models (PreConfig, arXiv:2403.09369) and practical tool‑augmented agent prototypes (Lu, preprints202604.1820.v1). Systematic discussions of verifier/tool tradeoffs and tool‑runtime reliability (WeClaw style and verifier taxonomies) informed our deterministic validator design (see 10.2139/ssrn.7317098 and 10.5220/0013221900003890). We adopt well‑documented generate‑validate‑repair motifs but purposely hold generation identical across arms to measure only post‑processing effects.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and core semantics. The study was preregistered as cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1 (artifact SHA‑256: 991674d5...). The design is paired binary with shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each task a single LLM generation was produced and reused verbatim by both pipelines (shared response files archived under execution/responses/task-<NNN>-shared-initial.txt; full hashes in execution manifest). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on a deterministic validator pass indicator. Planned n=300 pairs (150 simple, 150 complex), one shared generation per task, maximum model calls = 600. Model and orchestration. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256: 1acce925...). Adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator. Validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). It: (1) parses candidate commands into canonical configuration; (2) enforces per‑task workflow constraints (e.g., make_before_break, shutdown_configure_restore, group minima); (3) runs a lightweight topology simulator to compute final_state snapshots and reachability checks under injected fault scenarios; (4) emits structured validator_trace JSON (final_state, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes). All validator traces and scoring JSONs are archived under execution/scoring/*. The pre‑registered exclusion rules moved exact‑string matches to a public curated corpus out of the confirmatory set (none occurred in the confirmatory sample). Missingness and failures. Technical failures are logged; primary analysis used complete pairs (pairs with both outcomes present). The one missing pair (pair‑000269) arose from a failed shared_initial provider call and is recorded in execution/provider_calls/task-000269-shared-initial.json and the execution log (execution/execution_log.jsonl); the authoritative manifest entry and SHA‑256 appear in execution/execution_manifest.json (artifact hashes archived). Statistical analysis. Primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided on paired binary outcomes. Bootstrap percentile CI (10k resamples, seed=1729) for the paired difference. Secondary: descriptive cost metrics (model‑call counts, latencies). All analysis executors and parameters were frozen and archived (analysis/*).
sections.results: Execution and sample. Planned episodes: 600 (300 pairs). Completed episodes: 598 (two failed episodes constituted one missing pair); complete analyzable pairs = 299. Model calls used = 300 (one shared generation per task; execution manifest records provider call counts and per‑call hashes). Confirmatory contingency table (artifact: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 d77df43a...): n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Both baseline and guarded arms accepted the identical candidate in every analyzable pair. Estimated paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap (10k resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (degenerate due to zero discordant pairs). Representative episode diagnostics. The scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json; SHA‑256 listed in the execution manifest) contain normalized_response, validator_trace.final_state, parsed_command_count, required_command_count and difficulty tags (examples include patterns shutdown_configure_restore and make_before_break). Example shared candidate (task‑000001) is archived at execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 8f38c8be...), and the corresponding scoring JSONs show validator accepted the candidate after verifying workflow constraints (see analysis artifacts). Missingness/failure accounting. The single missing pair (pair‑000269) was produced by a failed shared_initial provider call; the failure and provider trace are recorded in execution/provider_calls/task-000269-shared-initial.json and the execution log file execution/execution_log.jsonl. The execution manifest lists these paths and their SHA‑256 hashes (authoritative artifact manifest: execution/execution_manifest.json). We do not invent per‑call error codes or timestamps in the manuscript beyond what the archived logs provide; the failure artifacts are available for audit at the recorded paths.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and scope. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics the deterministic validator verdict did not change when deterministic post‑processing (verifier + simulator) was applied to identical candidates. This factual outcome is narrow: it answers only whether post‑processing changes binary validator outcomes for identical candidates — it does not address whether tool‑augmented generation would produce higher‑quality or safer candidates. Ceiling effect and power. The preregistration assumed a baseline pass rate ≈0.60 to power detection of a 0.20 absolute improvement; the observed baseline success rate was 1.00, producing a ceiling effect that made the original minimally important effect unobservable. We therefore report exact counts, exact McNemar p‑value, and a degenerate bootstrap CI rather than interpreting the result as a powered null. Practical implications. Validators remain operationally valuable: they produce structured violation codes, final_state snapshots, and audit trails (see per‑episode validator_trace). When generator quality is lower, when independent per‑condition generation is used, or when repair loops are enabled, verifier and simulator components can (i) catch violations not visible to operators, (ii) supply granular failure codes for automated repair, and (iii) provide explainable audit records. Design lessons for follow‑ups. To measure the operational effect of tool‑augmented agentic generation we recommend: (1) independent per‑condition generation (no shared candidate), (2) adversarial/harder task strata to avoid ceiling effects, (3) multi‑model replication (different model families and multiple seeds), (4) inclusion of verifier‑guided repair loops with controlled repair budgets, and (5) evaluation metrics beyond binary pass/fail (e.g., simulated outage incidence, severity, and per‑task repair iterations). Reproducibility. Every number and claim here is traceable to archived artifacts with SHA‑256 hashes: raw responses (execution/responses/...), provider call traces (execution/provider_calls/...), validator scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/...), task manifests (execution/task_manifest.jsonl), execution manifest and full hash manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json). The analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/missingness_summary.csv) and analysis log are also archived; their SHA‑256s are recorded in the execution manifest and the analysis artifact summary.
sections.conclusion: In this preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired experiment holding generation fixed (shared_initial_candidate), deterministic verifier+simulator post‑processing did not alter deterministic validator pass/fail outcomes: both arms accepted the identical candidates in all 299 analyzable pairs (n11=299). The evidence is precise and fully archived, but the result is narrowly scoped: it does not speak to whether independent tool‑augmented generation would change generation quality or operational safety. We provide complete provenance to enable audit and reproduce the exact observed contingency; follow‑up experiments designed with independent per‑condition generation, adversarial tasks, and multi‑model replication are necessary to assess the practical operational value of tool‑augmented LLM agents for NetOps.

disclosure_statement: Mandatory Disclosure Statement: This manuscript and all reported results derive from an autonomous post‑lock research run governed by the immutable initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The experiment was preregistered as cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1 and frozen prior to execution (preregistration SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0). Declared LLM used: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; artifact SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Orchestration/adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0). Generation semantics required by the preregistration and executed here: shared_initial_candidate — for each paired task a single LLM candidate was produced and reused verbatim by both the baseline and guarded pipelines. The shared candidate raw response files are archived at execution/responses/task-<NNN>-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256s recorded under execution/*) and the provider call traces for these shared generation events are archived at execution/provider_calls/task-<NNN>-shared-initial.json (see execution manifest for the full per‑file hash list). Execution accounting: planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs); completed episodes = 598; failed episodes = 2 (forming one missing pair, pair‑000269); analyzable complete pairs = 299. The failed shared_initial provider call that produced the missing pair is recorded in the execution log (execution/execution_log.jsonl) and in the corresponding provider trace execution/provider_calls/task-000269-shared-initial.json; both paths and their SHA‑256 hashes are present in the authoritative execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json). All raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, analysis artifacts, and a full manifest of SHA‑256 artifact hashes are archived and serve as the authoritative source for every reported number (authoritative manifest path: execution/execution_manifest.json; see execution manifest for per‑file hashes). No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock; all manuscript numeric claims are grounded in these archived execution and analysis artifacts. This run followed the preregistered analysis plan (paired exact McNemar and bootstrap CI) and the missingness/contamination rules; any deviations are recorded in the execution/analysis manifests. The present manuscript reports only the narrowly preregistered estimand (effect of downstream tooling on identical LLM candidates) and explicitly does not claim results about independent tool‑augmented generation without further experiments.
limitations: The executed semantics fixed generation by reusing a single shared LLM candidate per task (shared_initial_candidate); results therefore answer only whether post‑generation tooling changes deterministic validator pass/fail for identical candidates, not whether independent tool‑augmented generation would produce different or safer outputs.
Tasks used deterministic synthetic topology templates and a lightweight simulator; external validity to vendor‑specific CLIs, device‑level idiosyncrasies, or production telemetry is limited.
Only one declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was used; results do not generalize across model families or scales without replication.

The deterministic validator enforces a curated rule set and workflow constraints; it cannot exhaustively model every hardware or vendor behavior and thus is an imperfect proxy for full production correctness.
A ceiling effect occurred: observed baseline success = 299/299, invalidating the preregistered power assumption and preventing detection of the originally targeted minimally important effect.
